record.paper_title: Open Questions in Cosmic-Ray Research at Ultrahigh Energies
record.original_question: For each candidate source class of ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays, over which energy ranges should the observed flux be modeled as steady and over which ranges should it be modeled as transient, given the ratio of propagation time to source emission time, magnetic-horizon effects, and energy losses? For gamma-ray bursts in particular, can they operate as efficient accelerators on the required timescales and remain viable ultrahigh-energy cosmic-ray sources?

evidence.quote: For UHECR sources, what deﬁnes whether a candidate object is classiﬁed as a transient or steady source is the ratio of the mean propagation timescale between sources to the source emission timescale, tprop/temiss.
These results leave unclear whether GRBs operate as efﬁcient particle accelerators (i.e. close to the Bohm limit), and on what timescale the acceleration takes place on.
It therefore remains unclear whether these objects can be considered as viable UHECR sources.
Indeed, it is possible for a source class to only achieve steady-state emission in a ﬁnite energy range, both below and above which the cosmic-ray ﬂux is only transient.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the population of astrophysical objects proposed as candidate sources of ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs), i.e. cosmic rays with energies above roughly 10^18 eV. For a given source class, define t_emiss as the characteristic timescale over which an individual source emits cosmic rays, and t_prop as the mean cosmic-ray propagation timescale between sources reaching an observer at Earth (which depends on energy through diffusion in extragalactic and Galactic magnetic fields, on the magnetic-horizon scale, and on energy losses such as photopion production, photodisintegration and adiabatic losses). Call the source class "steady" at energy E if t_prop(E)/t_emiss ≫ 1, so that many sources contribute to the observed flux at all times, and "transient" at energy E if t_prop(E)/t_emiss ≲ 1, so that the observed flux is dominated by individual bursts.

(a) For each candidate UHECR source class (e.g. active galactic nuclei, radio galaxies, starburst galaxies, tidal disruption events, gamma-ray bursts, magnetars, binary neutron-star mergers), determine, as a function of cosmic-ray energy E and primary species, the energy ranges over which the observed UHECR flux from that class should be modeled as steady and the energy ranges over which it should be modeled as transient, taking into account magnetic-horizon suppression and energy losses. In particular, characterize source classes for which steady-state emission is achieved only on a finite energy interval, with transient behavior both below and above it.

(b) Specializing to gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), determine whether GRBs can accelerate cosmic rays with efficiency close to the Bohm limit, on what timescale this acceleration occurs during the prompt and/or afterglow phases, and whether—given these acceleration properties together with the constraints from (a)—GRBs constitute viable sources of the observed UHECR flux.
artifact.status_search_result: As of 2025, the question remains open. Recent multi-messenger studies (2024–2025) continue to debate which source classes satisfy the steady-vs-transient requirements. Long GRBs (especially high-luminosity and ultra-long subclasses) are argued to satisfy the Hillas and multi-messenger criteria for transient UHECR acceleration, but their viability as the dominant UHECR source is not established; competing recent proposals (binary neutron-star mergers, magnetar transients, jetted TDEs) and the inability of standard candidates to fully explain the "standard source" phenomenon indicate the classification of source classes as steady/transient over various energy ranges, and the GRB acceleration efficiency, are still actively contested.

status_evidence.title: Multi-messenger constraints on transient accelerators of ultra-high energy cosmic rays
status_evidence.snippet: All subclasses of long GRBs fulfill the necessary criteria for UHECR acceleration; high-luminosity long GRBs reside in especially favorable parameter space.
status_evidence.claim: GRB viability as UHECR sources is still being constrained in 2025.

status_evidence.title: Ultrahigh Energy Cosmic Ray Production in Binary Neutron Star Mergers
status_evidence.snippet: The inability of AGN, long GRBs, TDEs and other previously suggested UHECR accelerators to satisfy the 'standard source' requirement prompted the suggestion that BNS mergers are the source of UHECRs.
status_evidence.claim: No consensus on which source class is steady/transient and viable; new candidates continue to be proposed.

status_evidence.title: Ultrahigh-Energy Cosmic Rays | Annual Reviews
status_evidence.snippet: Review of UHECR source candidates and outstanding open questions.
status_evidence.claim: The identification and steady/transient classification of UHECR sources remains an open problem in recent reviews.
